Introduction: For most people living with obesity, metabolic bariatric surgery (MBS) enables durable weight loss, improves a range of obesity-associated diseases, and increases longevity.1,2 However, up to 15% of people who undergo MBS experience suboptimal weight loss and therefore lesser improvement in health outcomes.3,4,5,6,7,8 The most common approach for treating suboptimal weight loss after MBS has been to revise or convert the index procedure, with the highest need for reintervention after adjustable gastric banding (AGB) followed by sleeve gastrectomy (SG), one anastomosis gastric bypass (OAGB), and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB).9 Revisional MBS has a higher risk of perioperative complications,10,11 and weight loss is typically lower than with primary procedures.11 Obesity management medications (OMMs) are rapidly evolving and are now providing short-term weight loss approaching that achieved by MBS.3 Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, which has been studied in 3 previous randomized clinical trials (RCTs) exploring the effect of combining OMMs and MBS. In the BARI-OPTIMISE study, 3.0 mg of liraglutide improved weight loss in individuals with poor weight loss after SG or RYGB with a sub-optimal GLP-1 nutrient-stimulated response.12 In the GRAVITAS study, 1.8 mg of liraglutide improved glycemia for those with suboptimal control of diabetes at least 12 months after RYGB or SG.13 In a trial focusing on patients who regained 10% total body weight loss (TBWL) or more after RYGB, 3.0 mg of liraglutide enabled an additional 8.8% (SD, −8.5%; range, −29.2% to 9.7%) TBWL compared with a gain of 1.1% (SD, 3.5%; range, −7.9% to 6.0%) in the placebo group at 56 weeks.14 These data suggest a role for OMMs for suboptimal weight loss after MBS, potentially avoiding riskier conversion MBS. Combining therapies might also enable less effective yet safer and reversible MBS procedures, such as AGB, to be reconsidered as a viable option. In this double-blinded RCT, we sought to study the effect of liraglutide on weight loss, health outcomes, and adverse effects in people who had achieved a stable, suboptimal weight loss 12 to 36 months after AGB or who had regained more than 5% TBW from their nadir. This was planned as an initial study to better understand how OMMs interact with MBS in a cohort accustomed to living with their AGB with a plan for a subsequent RCT that would focus on intervening earlier postoperatively when suboptimal weight loss was likely.15 Eligibility criteria were subsequently expanded to include people with suboptimal weight loss after other MBS. We hypothesized that 3.0 mg of liraglutide would improve weight loss after MBS.

Study Design and Setting: This prospective, double-blinded RCT was conducted at the Monash University Department of Surgery, Alfred Campus. Patients were recruited through 2 private practices associated with the Department of Surgery. All participants provided written informed consent. Ethical approval was obtained from the Avenue Human Research Ethics Committee, and the trial was prospectively registered with the ANZ Clinical Trials Registry. Consumers were not involved in the design of this trial. The trial protocol can be found in Supplement 1. Reporting followed the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) reporting guideline.18 The trial opened in July 2018 with the first participant enrolled on January 18, 2019. The Victorian state government COVID-19 pandemic response required all clinical trial activity at our center to halt from March 2020 until March 2023. After 2018, there was change in MBS practice leading to fewer AGB being performed at our center. In response, ethical approval to extend the study to include SG, OAGB, and RYGB was obtained in April 2022. Additional patients (all SG) were recruited between October 2022 to June 2023. The study was halted early on October 6, 2023, due to nonavailability of study medication.

Participant Recruitment and Care: Patients with anatomically correct AGB, SG, OAGB, or RYGB (confirmed with barium swallow and/or endoscopy) were invited to participate at 12 to 36 months after surgery if they had a body mass index BMI greater than 35 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared), were aged 20 to 65 years, and had achieved a stable weight (defined as a weight consistently within a 4-kg range during a 3-month period) with an excess body weight loss (EBWL; defined using a BMI threshold 25) of 25% to 40% or TBWL of 5% to 12% for AGB and EBWL of 25% to 60% or TBWL of 10% to 20% for SG, RYGB, and OAGB. These thresholds were determined because they were just below the mean result for these procedures.16 Patients were also invited to participate if they had regained 10% EBWL or 5% TBWL after reaching their nadir weight at any time point after surgery. All outcome data were collected by the trial coordinator. Measurements at baseline and 12 months included fasting insulin, glucose, and glycated hemoglobin; nutritional status (iron studies, B12, folate, and vitamin D); diseases associated with obesity as well as quality of life (36-Item Short-Form Medical Outcomes Study [SF-36] and Euro QOL 5-dimensions health utility survey), depression (Beck Depression Index), and general health focusing on quality of swallowing, reflux, and patient satisfaction using a validated questionnaire.17 Adherence was determined by assessing returned injection devices. Patients were excluded if they would not accept randomization; had a correctable mechanical issue with the bariatric procedure that explained suboptimal weight loss; had a history of multiple MBS procedures; had medical issues that contraindicated allocation to either treatment group, including tachycardia, acute myocardial infarction within the past 6 months, dementia, bulimia, active psychosis, pregnancy, lactation, illicit drug use, excessive alcohol intake, use of drugs known to affect body composition, cytotoxic drugs, internal malignant tumor, or major organ failure; had used a GLP-1 agonist in the previous 12 months; or were unable to provide informed consent. Patients with risk factors for pancreatitis (eg, drugs, excessive alcohol intake, and known symptomatic gallstones) were also excluded. Due to nausea being an expected adverse effect of liraglutide, leading to the possibility that an AGB would need to be deflated immediately, patients living more than 1 hour from the study center were also excluded.

Randomization: Participants were randomized 1:1 to either liraglutide or placebo. Both medications were provided by the manufacturer (Novo Nordisk). The treating practitioner, coordinators, and patients were unaware of program assignment. Randomization was performed in blocks of 6 or 8 using a computer-generated process by the Monash University School of Public Health and Preventative Medicine data center.

Procedures: All participants were reviewed by a dietician and a bariatric surgeon or physician after enrollment and undertook a common program focusing on improved eating styles and behaviors. Participants were clinically reviewed by a bariatric physician or surgeon monthly. Liraglutide (6 mg/mL [3 mL]) or placebo (saline) was provided in prefilled multidose disposable pens and self-administered daily. Participants were instructed to escalate the dose from 0.6 mg in week 1 by 0.6 mg/d per week until 3.0 mg was reached by week 5.

Outcomes: The primary end point was the percentage of weight loss achieved after enrollment at 12 months. Baseline weight was defined as weight at the screening visit. Secondary end points included measures of safety, including mortality, adverse effects (grade 3 or higher), and need for reoperation for a complication of the MBS procedure; measures of health benefit, including improvement in diabetes and hypertension; measures of nutrition, including iron, vitamins B12, B1, and D, calcium, and albumin; measures of function and well-being, including SF-36, Beck Depression Index, Euro QOL 5-dimensions health utility survey, quality of swallowing, reflux, and satisfaction questionnaire,17 and drug adherence.

Sample Size: Clinical trials have found that 3.0 mg of liraglutide induces a mean 6% TBWL more than placebo. With a 2-sided α = .05 and β = 0.8, we would require a sample size of 34 (17 in each arm) to detect a difference equivalent to 1 SD. Allowing for 50% dropouts in line with other drug trials we have conducted, we sought to recruit 48 patients (24 in each arm).

Statistical Analysis: All data from the study were managed by the data manager within the Monash University Department of Surgery, Alfred Campus, who was independent of the trial. The preliminary primary analysis of all data from the trial was performed on July 15, 2024, according to the intention-to-treat principle. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics, as well as quality-of-life data, were compared between treatment arms using the t test, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, or χ2 test for equal proportions, as appropriate. A longitudinal analysis was performed using the PROC MIXED procedure in SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute) to estimate weight measures (weight, BMI, and percentage of TBWL) accounting for missing data, with each participant treated as a random effect. Models were fitted using main effects for treatment, time, and an interaction between treatment and time to ascertain whether the treatment groups behaved differently over time. To account for confounding effects, the models were further adjusted for the type of operation. Time was treated as a categorical variable to facilitate specific comparisons. The results from the mixed-effects models were reported as least-squares means (SEs). All observed data were considered for analysis, with the mixed-effects model assuming noninformative dropout such that the probability of dropout may depend on a participant’s previous response but not on current or future responses. No adjustment was made for multiple outcome comparisons. A 2-sided P < .05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed with the SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc).

Study Participants: There were 24 participants in each arm of the study. The mean (SD) age of participants in the liraglutide arm was 48.7 (10.5) years with 22 (92%) female and 2 (8%) male. The mean (SD) age of participants in the placebo arm was 43.6 (11.4) years with 20 (83%) female and 4 (17%) male. The first patient was enrolled January 18, 2019 (Figure 1) with 21 patients with AGB commencing the study by March 2020. In March 2020 our study was impacted by the first of 7 lockdowns (262 days) that were mandated in Victoria, Australia, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. No clinical trial activity was subsequently permitted on site at our center until March 2023. During this time, a change in practice meant there were no longer sufficient AGB patients eligible for the study. An additional 27 patients (all SG) were recruited between October 2022 to June 2023 (Figure 1). The study was halted early on October 6, 2023, due to nonavialability of study medication. This meant that 19 patients could not complete the 12-month time of the trial. An overview of the available data are shown in eFigure in Supplement 1. Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The mean (SD) TBWL from the day of MBS was 16.9% (6.8%) for liraglutide-treated participants and 17.3% (7.1%) in the placebo group. The mean (SE) weight at day of commencement of study therapy was 104.4 (3.3) kg in the liraglutide group and 101.9 (3.3) kg in the placebo group. No participants were receiving glucose-lowering medication. The mean (SD) time to enrollment after MBS was 1.7 (0.5) years in the liraglutide group and 1.5 (0.5) years in the placebo group.

Weight Loss Outcomes: Mean (SE) percentage of TWL at 12 months was 4.4% (0.9%) for liraglutide, whereas weight increased by a mean (SE) of 1.4% (1.0%) in the placebo group (P < .001). At 6 months, mean (SE) weight loss was 4.6 (1.0) kg for liraglutide and 0.4 (1.1) kg for placebo (P = .005). At 12 months, mean (SE) weight loss in the liraglutide and placebo groups was 5.7 (1.1) vs −1.4 (1.2) kg (P < .001), with a between-group difference of 7.1 kg (95% CI, 3.9-10.3 kg). The mixed-effects model showed consistent weight loss in the liraglutide group (Figure 2A and B) during the study period. The treatment effect remained consistent after adjusting for operation type (eTables 1-4 in Supplement 2).

Changes in Measures of Health and Nutrition: At 12 months, mean (SE) diastolic blood pressure increased in the liraglutide group (78 [9] vs 82 [6] mm Hg; P = .02) but did not change in the placebo group. There were no other significant changes in any other health outcomes both within and between the treatment groups (Table 1).

Changes in Quality of Life and Quality of Swallowing: At 12 months, the liraglutide group (n = 19) had lower mean (SE) SF-36 pain scores than the placebo group (70.4 [4.4] vs 86.3 [0.5]; P = .04), whereas the physical functioning mean (SE) score was higher in the placebo group (92.5 [6.2] vs 76.1 [4.5]; P = .04). When compared with baseline, however, at 12 months there was no significant within group differences between any patient-reported measures (Figure 3; eTables 5 and 6 in Supplement 2).

Medication Use: The mean (SE) overall dose of medication self-administered in the liraglutide group was 2.43 (0.65) mg compared with 2.20 (0.83) mg in the placebo group (P = .003). The mean (SE) doses of liraglutide were 2.26 (0.72) mg for people with AGB and 2.56 (0.53) mg for people with SG (P < .001). In the placebo group, the mean (SE) doses were 2.12 (0.82) mg for people with AGB and 2.33 (0.83) mg for people with SG (P = .06) (Table 2). No grade 3 or higher adverse events were reported during the trial.

Discussion: In this single-center, double-blinded RCT, liraglutide provided greater weight loss at 12 months than placebo in a cohort of patients with a suboptimal response to MBS (AGB or SG), with no serious adverse events and no adverse impact on health, nutrition, and well-being. Despite 3.0 mg being the approved dose for weight management, lower doses were often used, particularly in people who had AGB. SG is currently the most popular MBS globally,9 with a weighted mean percentage of TBWL at 10 years after the procedure of 24.4% (range, 17.0%-36.9%) and a 7.8% to 26.9% need for conversion surgery for suboptimal weight loss or recurrent weight gain.19 AGB was previously commonly performed,20 particularly in Australia. Although AGB is safe and reversible, weight loss is less, with a weighted mean EBWL at 10 years after the procedure of 45.9% (range, 27.0%-66.0%), which equates to percentage of TBWL of approximately 18% to 20%. There is a high need for reoperation, ranging from 8% to 78%, although conversion surgery for suboptimal weight loss or recurrent weight gain has not been well reported.2 Converting one MBS to another carries a higher risk of mortality9 and morbidity,21,22 and the weight loss provided is often more modest than with a primary procedure of the same type,23 meaning that when conversional surgery is being considered for suboptimal weight loss, the potential benefits need to be carefully weighed against the increased surgical risk. On the basis of these current data, it is possible that the need for conversion surgery could be avoided or delayed by the addition of OMMs. There is great heterogeneity in weight response to all obesity therapies, including MBS.3 We have previously demonstrated that by 3 months after AGB it is possible to estimate who will have a suboptimal response.15 Weight loss at 3 months is also an important factor associated with suboptimal responses after SG.24 Our demonstration of safety and efficacy of OMMs after MBS suggests that OMMs might be used earlier after MBS rather than waiting for suboptimal weight loss or weight regain. The safety and efficacy of early OMM treatment warrant testing in future studies. The global use of AGB has decreased markedly in the past 15 years due to less predictable weight loss, higher reoperation rates, and need for intensive follow-up.9 AGB remains, however, a safe MBS option and is easily reversible, features valued by selected group of patients.2 Many of the difficulties encountered after the AGB related to overtightening of the band.25,26 It is possible that combining an OMM with AGB could deliver improved weight loss, with less fluid in the band required, reducing long-term complications. Although this would increase the number of choices available to people seeking weight loss, additional trials are required to test this possibility. Quality of life after MBS typically improves, although most domains remain lower than for people who have never had obesity.27 The quality-of-life domains reported in this study are similar to ones we have previously reported in patients who had undergone either SG or AGB for regurgitation, reflux, and dysphagia, although the physical domains of the SF-36 were higher.28 Although the SF-36 physical functioning scores were lower at 12 months in the group treated with liraglutide, there was no significant difference to placebo when comparing the change from commencement of the trial. There was no deleterious effect of liraglutide on quality of eating and swallowing, which is important given that GLP analogues delay gastric emptying and increase reflux.29 The approved dose of liraglutide for weight management is 3.0 mg/d. Although study patients were asked to escalate their doses according to the standard schedule, the mean dose was less than 3.0 mg at all time points. Data on why doses were not escalated as expected were not systematically collected, and the study was not sufficiently powered to enable stratification by dose achieved. It is possible that patients were happy with the weight loss effect at lower doses or that adverse effects limited further escalation. Additional studies should confirm whether the full dose of OMMs is required in conjunction with MBS.

Limitations: There are several limitations to this study. The timeline was much longer than projected due to the COVID-19 pandemic. This impacted our ability to collect all weight data in the clinic. The nonavailability of placebo in 2023 led to premature cessation of the trial, leaving several patients unable to complete 12-month follow-up. Although this was accounted for statistically, it would have been preferable to complete the study. The inclusion criteria were expanded due to a change in practice during the trial; however, this strengthens the applicability of the study to areas outside Australia where AGB is not commonly performed. Although we aimed to recruit people who had undergone both RYGB and OAGB, we had no patients in our practice who fulfilled the inclusion criteria. This may reflect better weight loss that is typically seen with these procedures or an intrinsic bias in our practice because we performed fewer of these operations as primary procedures at the time that would have impacted recruitment.30 The study was powered around the primary outcome of weight loss not secondary outcomes.

Conclusions: The advent of effective OMMs is reframing the place of MBS in the obesity treatment paradigm. Combining OMMs with MBS affords the opportunity to increase weight loss for those with a suboptimal initial response or weight regain, potentially avoiding conversion surgery. OMMs might also enable more frequent use of less invasive, reversible procedures, such as AGB. Data from this study will contribute to our understanding of these important clinical issues.

title: Improved health-related quality of life with tirzepatide versus semaglutide in adults with obesity or overweight from the SURMOUNT-5 trial.
abstract: AIMS: In SURMOUNT-5, tirzepatide led to greater body weight (BW) reduction versus semaglutide in adults with obesity without T2D. Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) with tirzepatide versus semaglutide in SURMOUNT-5 was evaluated. | MATERIALS AND METHODS: This analysis included on-treatment data from participants who received ≥1 dose of tirzepatide or semaglutide at their maximum tolerated dose. Changes in prespecified Short Form-36 Health Survey Version 2 (SF-36v2) norm-based scores for the Physical Component Summary (PCS), Mental Component Summary (MCS), and each domain, Patient Health Questionnaire-9, and Patient Global Impression of Status for Physical Activity scores were assessed at Week 72. Post hoc analysis of changes in SF-36v2 scores in participants with limited baseline physical function and by BW reduction thresholds was assessed at Week 72. | RESULTS: Baseline scores were similar between treatments and among BW reduction categories. At Week 72, PCS scores improved from baseline with both treatments (p < 0.001). However, MCS scores did not show significant improvements from baseline (p > 0.05 for both treatment arms). All domain scores improved (p ≤ 0.008), with greater improvements in General Health (GH) with tirzepatide versus semaglutide (5.45 vs. 4.20; p = 0.003). Participants with limited physical function improved in PCS, Physical Functioning (PF), and GH with tirzepatide versus semaglutide (p ≤ 0.025). Higher BW reductions were associated with more improvement in PCS, PF, Role-Physical, Bodily Pain (BP), GH, and Vitality scores with tirzepatide and semaglutide (pooled). | CONCLUSIONS: HRQoL improved with tirzepatide and semaglutide, with greater improvement in GH with tirzepatide, especially in participants with limited baseline physical function. Participants who lost the most BW showed the greatest improvements in PF, BP, and GH.

ABSTRACT: In SURMOUNT‐5, tirzepatide led to greater body weight (BW) reduction versus semaglutide in adults with obesity without T2D. Changes in prespecified Short Form‐36 Health Survey Version 2 (SF‐36v2) norm‐based scores for the Physical Component Summary (PCS), Mental Component Summary (MCS), and each domain, Patient Health Questionnaire‐9, and Patient Global Impression of Status for Physical Activity scores were assessed at Week 72. Post hoc analysis of changes in SF‐36v2 scores in participants with limited baseline physical function and by BW reduction thresholds was assessed at Week 72. Baseline scores were similar between treatments and among BW reduction categories. At Week 72, PCS scores improved from baseline with both treatments (p < 0.001). However, MCS scores did not show significant improvements from baseline (p > 0.05 for both treatment arms). All domain scores improved (p ≤ 0.008), with greater improvements in General Health (GH) with tirzepatide versus semaglutide (5.45 vs. 4.20; p = 0.003). Participants with limited physical function improved in PCS, Physical Functioning (PF), and GH with tirzepatide versus semaglutide (p ≤ 0.025). Higher BW reductions were associated with more improvement in PCS, PF, Role‐Physical, Bodily Pain (BP), GH, and Vitality scores with tirzepatide and semaglutide (pooled). HRQoL improved with tirzepatide and semaglutide, with greater improvement in GH with tirzepatide, especially in participants with limited baseline physical function. Participants who lost the most BW showed the greatest improvements in PF, BP, and GH.

 Therefore, addressing both the physical and mental components of obesity is crucial for effective and sustained treatment. In clinical trials, these components can be assessed using patient‐reported health‐related quality of life measures, which provide a comprehensive overview of the effectiveness of treatment and ensure that the patients are experiencing meaningful improvements in their daily lives.
13
, 
14 First generation obesity management medications (OMMs), including orlistat, phentermine/topiramate extended release, bupropion/naltrexone sustained release, and liraglutide, provide proven effectiveness and tolerability
15
 and improvements in health‐related quality of life outcomes.
16
, 
17
, 
18
, 
19
 However, body weight reduction averages less than 10%.
20
, 
21
 Second‐generation OMMs, including tirzepatide, a single molecule, dual glucose‐dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor and glucagon‐like peptide‐1 (GLP‐1) receptor agonist,
22
 and semaglutide, a selective GLP‐1 receptor agonist,
23
 are the first two approved highly effective OMMs
21
 that contribute to greater magnitudes of body weight reduction compared to their first‐generation predecessors.
24 In the placebo‐controlled Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with Obesity (STEP) 1–5 clinical trials with treatment durations ranging from 68 to 104 weeks, once weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg achieved superior and clinically meaningful reductions in body weight ranging from 9.6% to 16.0% compared with placebo (mean reduction ranging from 2.4% to 5.7%) and with clinically meaningful improvements in physical functioning in participants with obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes (T2D).
25
, 
26
, 
27
, 
28
 Furthermore in STEP 8, a 68‐week trial that assessed the efficacy and safety of once weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg to once‐daily liraglutide 3.0 mg (both with diet and physical activity), semaglutide‐treated participants demonstrated superior body weight reduction of 15.8% compared to a reduction of 6.4% with liraglutide, with a significantly greater proportion achieving body weight reduction thresholds ≥10%, ≥15% and ≥20% with semaglutide.
29
 Although health‐related quality of life outcomes were measured, the data have not been published to‐date. In the phase 3 randomized, placebo‐controlled SURMOUNT trials, superior body weight reductions ranging from 13% to 26% were observed with tirzepatide in participants with obesity (body mass index [BMI] ≥30 kg/m2) or overweight (BMI ≥27 kg/m2 with at least one weight‐related comorbid condition), with or without T2D.
30
, 
31
, 
32
, 
33
 Furthermore, treatment with tirzepatide was associated with improved health‐related quality of life compared to placebo in people with overweight or obesity, with and without T2D.
34
, 
35
, 
36
, 
37
 In general, larger improvements in health‐related quality of life were associated with higher weight reduction thresholds, and greater improvements in physical functioning were observed among individuals with baseline limitations. In SURMOUNT‐5, the first head‐to‐head trial of highly effective, second generation OMMs, treatment with once weekly tirzepatide versus semaglutide resulted in superior reductions in body weight (22% vs. 15%) and waist circumference (20 vs. 15 cm) at week 72.
38 Herein, we assessed overall changes in health‐related quality of life with tirzepatide versus semaglutide in adults with obesity or overweight from the SURMOUNT‐5 trial.

Trial design and participants: Study design, full inclusion and exclusion criteria, and primary results are published.
38
 Briefly, SURMOUNT‐5 was a phase 3b multicenter, randomized, parallel‐arm, open‐label, controlled, 72‐week trial that included adults aged 18 years or older, with a BMI ≥30 kg/m2 or BMI ≥27 kg/m2 with at least one weight‐related complication (hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, or cardiovascular disease), and experiencing at least one unsuccessful dietary effort for weight reduction. Key exclusion criteria included a diabetes diagnosis, past or planned surgical treatment for obesity, and treatment with a medication for weight reduction or a GLP‐1 receptor agonist or a change in body weight >5 kg within 3 months prior to screening. Participants were randomized (1:1) to once weekly tirzepatide maximum tolerated dose (MTD, 10 mg or 15 mg) or semaglutide MTD (1.7 mg or 2.4 mg). Dose escalation was consistent with both medications' approved Prescribing Information in the United States (USPI). Participants were intended to aim to reach the maximum dose, but the lower dose was allowed in case of persistent gastrointestinal intolerance. The SURMOUNT‐5 trial (clinicaltrials.gov identifier, NCT05822830) was conducted in accordance with the International Conference on Harmonization Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice and the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided signed informed consent, and protocols were approved by local ethical review boards. The study protocol and statistical analysis plan for the SURMOUNT‐5 trial are published.
38

Endpoints: Prespecified analyses of Short Form‐36 Health Survey Version 2 (SF‐36v2) norm‐based scores, which included changes from baseline in Physical Component Summary (PCS) and Mental Component Summary (MCS), as well as each individual domain: Physical Functioning, Role‐Physical, Bodily Pain, General Health, Vitality, Social Functioning, Role‐Emotional, Mental Health were assessed at Week 72. The SF‐36v2 acute form is a 36‐item, validated, patient‐reported measure designed to assess eight domains of functioning and health that are also combined to obtain two component summary scores (i.e., PCS and MCS).
39
 The SF‐36v2 acute form was administered at baseline and at Weeks 36 and 72. Changes in the presence and severity of depression symptoms determined by prespecified assessment of categorical shift from baseline in Patient Health Questionnaire‐9 (PHQ‐9) score at Week 72. The PHQ‐9 is a well‐validated, self‐report screening tool that screens for the presence and intensity of symptoms of MDD, using a scale anchored by ‘0’ (not at all) to ‘3’ (nearly every day).
40
 Respondents rate their experience of each of nine symptoms over the past 2 weeks with total scores ranging from 0 to 4, 5 to 9, 10 to 14, 15 to 19, and ≥20, suggesting no/minimal, mild, moderate, moderately severe, and severe symptoms of depression, respectively. Scores of ≥15 typically trigger referral to a mental health professional. The PHQ‐9 was administered at baseline and at Weeks 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 36, 48, 52, 60, 72, and at 4 weeks post‐treatment. The proportion of participants with improved physical limitations determined by prespecified assessment of categorical shift from baseline in Patient Global Impression of Status (PGI‐S) for Physical Activity score at Week 72. The PGI‐S is a patient‐rated questionnaire that assesses the current severity of physical limitations due to obesity (i.e., during the past week) and is rated on a 5‐point scale ranging from 1 ‘not at all limited’ to 5 ‘extremely limited’.
41
 Impaired physical function was defined as a score of 3 or above (i.e., moderately limited, very much limited, or extremely limited) and was administered at baseline and at Weeks 36 and 72. Post hoc analyses of changes in SF‐36v2 norm‐based scores in participants with limited PGI‐S at baseline and changes in SF‐36v2 norm‐based scores by body weight reduction thresholds (<5%, <10%, 10 to <20%, 20% to <30%, and ≥30%) with tirzepatide and semaglutide (pooled) at Week 72 were also assessed.

Statistical analyses: Data while on treatment from all participants who received at least one dose of study drug were used for these analyses. Changes from baseline in SF‐36 v2 norm‐based scores: PCS, MCS, and each domain were analyzed using a mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) analysis with the following fixed effects: treatment group (tirzepatide 15 mg or MTD, and semaglutide 2.4 mg or MTD), visit, and treatment‐by‐visit interaction, prediabetes status at randomization, sex, and BMI category. Baseline value was also included as a covariate. Missing data were addressed by the MMRM model, which is based on the missing at random assumption. No explicit imputation methods for missing data were employed. Treatment comparisons were not adjusted for multiplicity.

Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics: The baseline demographics and clinical characteristics for the overall population were well balanced across the treatment groups (Table S1). Overall mean baseline age was 44.7 years, duration of obesity was 15.6 years, body weight was 113.0 kg, and BMI was 39.4 kg/m2. The majority of participants were female (64.7%) and White (76.1%). A total of 56.7% of participants reported prediabetes at randomization and 50.1% had obesity‐related multimorbidity (≥2 obesity‐related complications). Furthermore, baseline SF‐36v2 norm‐based scores were well balanced across treatment groups for the overall population and among participants with limited physical activity (Table S2).

Categorical shift in PHQ‐9 total scores: PHQ‐9 total scores were assessed to evaluate degree of depression severity following treatment with tirzepatide compared with semaglutide, with a higher score indicating more severe depression (Table 1). Overall, the proportion of participants with post‐baseline shifts in PHQ‐9 total scores indicates that the onset or worsening of depressive symptoms was similar among the tirzepatide and semaglutide groups. At Week 72, among the 290 (77.5%) tirzepatide‐treated participants who reported no/minimal symptoms of depression at baseline (score, 0–4), 245 (65.5%) remained in this category, 35 (9.4%) participants reported mild symptoms (score, 5–9) at one or more assessment, 4 (1.1%) acknowledged moderate symptoms (score, 10–14), 1 (0.3%) reported moderately‐severe symptoms (score, 15–19) and none reported severe symptoms (score, 20–27). Among the 288 (76.6%) semaglutide‐treated participants who reported no/minimal symptoms of depression at baseline (score, 0–4), 251 (66.8%) remained in this category, 32 (8.5%) participants reported mild symptoms (score, 5–9), 2 (0.5%) acknowledged moderate symptoms (score, 10–14), 1 (0.3) reported moderately‐severe symptoms (score, 15–19) and none reported severe symptoms (score, 20–27). The majority of participants from both treatment groups who reported mild to moderate depression at baseline, reported no/minimal symptoms of depression at Week 72. No participants reported moderately‐severe symptoms of depression at baseline. However, one participant from the tirzepatide group reported severe symptoms of depression at baseline and was discontinued from the study due to inadvertent enrolment. At any time during the treatment period, 46 (12.5%) participants in the tirzepatide group and 41 (11.0%) in the semaglutide group experienced an increase in depression category, including 11 (3.1%) tirzepatide‐treated participants and 9 (2.5%) in semaglutide‐treated participants increasing from no/mild symptoms of depression to moderate, moderately severe or severe depression, and 1 (1.2%) tirzepatide‐treated participants and 1 (1.1%) semaglutide‐treated participants increasing from mild or moderate symptoms of depression to moderately severe or severe depression (Table S3). During the study, a PHQ‐9 score of ≥15 was a clinical consideration for permanent discontinuation of the study drug. No participants discontinued from the study due to PHQ‐9 scores.

Categorical shifts in PGI‐S scores: Categorical shifts in physical limitations as assessed by PGI‐S scores are presented in Table 2. Overall, the proportion of participants with post‐baseline shifts in PGI‐S scores indicates similar improvements in physical limitations among the tirzepatide and semaglutide groups. Among the 154 (41.2%) tirzepatide‐treated participants who reported ‘not at all limited’ at baseline, 110 (29.4%) remained in this category, 9 (2.4%) participants reported ‘a little limited’ at one or more assessment, 1 (0.3%) acknowledged ‘moderately limited’, 1 (0.3) reported ‘very much limited’, and none reported ‘extremely limited’ at Week 72. Among the 173 (46.0%) semaglutide‐treated participants who reported ‘not at all limited’ at baseline, 124 (33.0%) remained in this category, 7 (1.9%) participants reported ‘a little limited’ at one or more assessment, 3 (0.8%) acknowledged ‘moderately limited’, none reported ‘very much limited’, and 1 (0.3%) reported ‘extremely limited’ at Week 72. The majority of participants from both treatment groups who reported ‘a little limited’ or more at baseline, shifted to ‘not at all limited’ at Week 72.

SF‐36v2 acute form outcomes: Changes from baseline physical and mental health outcomes assessed by SF‐36v2 norm‐based scores are reported in Figures 1 and S1. At Week 72, statistically significant improvements from baseline in SF‐36v2 scores were observed across all domains in both treatment groups (p < 0.001 with tirzepatide p ≤ 0.008 with semaglutide) (Figure 1A). Improvements in SF‐36v2 scores did not differ between treatment groups, except for a significantly greater improvement in General Health with tirzepatide compared with semaglutide (estimated treated difference [95% confidence interval]: 1.25 [0.43, 2.06]; p = 0.003). Furthermore, PCS scores significantly improved from baseline with tirzepatide and semaglutide at Week 72 (p < 0.001, both treatment groups) and did not differ between groups (0.70 [−0.03, 1.44]; p = 0.061) (Figure 1B). MCS scores did not differ with tirzepatide or semaglutide (0.34 [−0.45, 1.13]; p = 0.397) (Figure 1B).

SF‐36v2 outcomes by baseline PGI‐S status: Post hoc analyses of changes in SF‐36v2 norm‐based scores were further assessed in a subgroup of participants who reported limited physical activity at baseline and are reported in Figure 2. At Week 72, statistically significant improvements from baseline in SF‐36v2 scores were observed across all domains (p < 0.001 with tirzepatide and p ≤ 0.002 with semaglutide) (Figure 2A). Improvements in SF‐36v2 scores did not differ between treatment groups, except for a significantly greater improvement with tirzepatide in Physical Functioning (estimated treated difference [95% confidence interval]: 1.19 [0.15, 2.24]; p = 0.025) and General Health (1.46 [0.29, 2.63]; p = 0.015). Furthermore, in participants with limited physical activity function at baseline, PCS scores significantly improved from baseline with tirzepatide and semaglutide at Week 72 (p < 0.001, both groups) and were significantly greater with tirzepatide compared with semaglutide (1.33 [0.23, 2.43]; p = 0.018) (Figure 2B). MCS scores did not differ with tirzepatide or semaglutide treatment (0.46 [−0.65, 1.58]; p = 0.414) (Figure 2B).

SF‐36v2 outcomes by body weight reduction thresholds: Post hoc analyses of changes in SF‐36v2 norm‐based scores by body reduction thresholds from pooled tirzepatide‐ and semaglutide‐treated participants (N = 750) are reported in Figure 3. At Week 72, 41 (5.5%) achieved body weight reduction <5%, 121 (16.1%) achieved body weight reduction <10%, 208 (27.7%) achieved body weight reduction 10 to <20%, 173 (23.1%) achieved body weight reduction 20 to <30%, and 99 (13.2%) achieved body weight reduction ≥30%. Overall, baseline SF‐36v2 scores were well balanced among body weight reduction subgroups. Higher body weight reduction was associated with greater improvements in Physical Functioning, Role‐Physical, Bodily Pain, General Health, and Vitality scores with tirzepatide and semaglutide (pooled) (Figure 3A,B). Similarly, greater improvements in PCS scores were observed among participants who met higher body weight reduction thresholds (Figure 3C). Other domains did not follow the same pattern.

DISCUSSION: In the SURMOUNT‐5 trial, both treatment groups demonstrated significant improvements in health‐related quality of life, with tirzepatide yielding greater improvement in the General Health domain compared to semaglutide. Overall, participants who achieved higher body weight reductions reported greater improvements in PCS, as well as the Physical Functioning, Role‐Physical, Bodily Pain, General Health, and Vitality domains. Health‐related quality of life improved with both treatments in participants with limited physical functioning at baseline, with greater improvements in the Physical Functioning domain and in the PCS reported with tirzepatide compared with semaglutide. In general, participants from SURMOUNT‐5 treated with tirzepatide or semaglutide exhibited favourable outcomes in physical health. However, improvement in mental health parameters, as indicated by the MCS, was not observed in either treatment group, despite significant improvements in individual Vitality, Social Functioning, Role‐Emotional, and Mental Health domain scores. Additionally, a similar number of participants experienced onset or worsening of depressive symptoms in both treatment groups. While systematic review and meta‐analyses of selective GLP‐1 RAs
42
 and tirzepatide
43
 have not found increased risk for psychiatric adverse effects, people with obesity do have increased mental illness, most commonly depression and anxiety, and require ongoing monitoring. Both treatment groups demonstrated comparable shifts in PGI‐S scores, with the majority of participants remaining in or shifting to the ‘not at all limited’ category. These findings were noted alongside superior clinical outcomes for reduction in body weight and waist circumference with tirzepatide compared with semaglutide.
38 The current findings are consistent with the placebo‐controlled SURMOUNT trials in participants with obesity, with and without T2D. In SURMOUNT‐1, tirzepatide (10 or 15 mg) was associated with greater improvements in SF‐36v2 Physical Functioning at Week 72 compared with placebo in participants with obesity without T2D.
30
, 
34
 Quality of life also improved to a greater extent with tirzepatide compared with placebo following over 3 years of treatment in participants with obesity and prediabetes, with improvements in all domains of the SF‐36 and the IWQOL‐Lite‐CT, and most notably physical function.
44
 Similarly in SURMOUNT‐2 in participants with obesity and T2D, greater improvements in health‐related quality of life were observed particularly among those who achieved greater body weight reduction or had physical function limitations at baseline.
35
 In SURMOUNT‐3, improved health‐related quality of life was reported with tirzepatide treatment compared with placebo in adults with obesity/overweight who had already lost ≥5% body weight with intensive lifestyle intervention
36
 and, more recently in SURMOUNT‐4, participants who continued to receive tirzepatide MTD reported significant and sustained improvement from baseline in all domains of health‐related quality of life when compared to those who switched to placebo.
37
 Furthermore, improvements in health‐related quality of life observed with semaglutide were generally consistent with the placebo‐controlled STEP clinical trials. In STEP 1, treatment with semaglutide 2.4 mg resulted in physical functioning scores for SF‐36v2, as well as PCS and MCS scores, and greater improvement in physical functioning scores for The Impact of Weight on Quality of Life‐Lite‐Clinical Trials (IWQOL‐Lite‐CT) compared with placebo in participants with overweight or obesity.
25
 Similarly in STEP 2, greater improvements in physical functioning scores for SF‐36v2 and IWQOL‐Lite‐CT were observed with semaglutide compared with placebo in participants with obesity and T2D.
26
 However in STEP 3, when added an adjunct to intensive behavioural therapy with initial low‐calorie diet, the improvement in PCS scores did not differ between semaglutide and placebo groups, whereas the MCS score favoured semaglutide.
27
 Among participants who completed a 20‐week run‐in period with semaglutide 2.4 mg, maintaining treatment with semaglutide compared with switching to placebo resulted in improved SF‐36 physical functioning score.
28
 In a recently published post hoc analysis of STEP 1–4, semaglutide 2.4 mg significantly improved physical functioning, with a greater proportion of participants achieving meaningful changes as perceived by individual participants compared with placebo, and demonstrated beneficial effects on weight‐ and health‐related quality of life beyond physical functioning.
45 A key strength of the study is the head‐to‐head comparison of the two currently most efficacious OMMs. Additionally, its assessment of the maximum tolerated dose for tirzepatide and semaglutide, reflecting real‐world clinical practice more closely than that of a fixed dose regimen. Additionally, study participants represented a diverse population living with obesity, including a higher number of participants who self‐reported as Black race or Hispanic or Latino ethnicity. Study limitations include geographical restriction to the United States and Puerto Rico and that the study was not blinded, thereby potentially introducing bias in data collection and patient‐reported outcomes. However, the current findings are consistent with those previously reported in blinded trials, suggesting generalizability of the results. Additionally, the study was not powered for exploratory endpoints and these endpoints were not adjusted for multiplicity. In conclusion, in the SURMOUNT‐5 trial, tirzepatide MTD demonstrated greater body weight reduction compared with semaglutide MTD. In this analysis improvements in health‐related quality of life were observed with both tirzepatide and semaglutide, with greater improvement in GH with tirzepatide especially in those with physical function limitations at baseline. Overall, adults who achieved greater body weight reductions demonstrated larger improvements in health‐related quality of life. Findings from this study support the role of both tirzepatide or semaglutide in the potential improvements in health‐related quality of life in addition to achieving beneficial clinical outcomes in adults with overweight or obesity.

title: Adjunctive Semaglutide in Patients Undergoing Intragastric Balloon for Weight Loss: 12-Month Prospective Comparative Study.

The aim of this study is to evaluate the synergistic effects of the intragastric balloon and semaglutide on weight reduction and weight regain. | METHODS: In this prospective, randomized cohort, adults between the ages of 18 and 65, with a BMI of at least 27 kg/m², were assigned to one of two treatment groups: IGB only or IGB + semaglutide. Subcutaneous injections of semaglutide were administered with increasing dosages on a weekly basis in the second month and were continued after the removal of the intragastric balloon. All participants were monitored, and results were recorded at 3, 6, and 12 months. | RESULTS: Forty patients completed the study (n = 20 per group). The IGB + semaglutide group lost more weight than the IGB only group at 3, 6, and 12 months, with statistically significant differences at 6 months (29.09 ± 3.45 kg vs. 18.35 ± 2.80 kg, p < 0.001) and 12 months (33.03 ± 3.55 kg vs. 15.56 ± 2.50 kg, p < 0.001). This combined therapeutic approach may provide an additional non-invasive intervention that provides optimal results and long-term weight loss maintenance.

TITLE: Adjunctive Semaglutide in Patients Undergoing Intragastric Balloon for Weight Loss: 12-Month Prospective Comparative Study

ABSTRACT: Given the global increase in obesity prevalence, there has been an emergence of a multitude of treatment options, specifically less invasive operations, like intragastric balloons, and pharmaceutical treatments like semaglutide. The aim of this study is to evaluate the synergistic effects of the intragastric balloon and semaglutide on weight reduction and weight regain. In this prospective, randomized cohort, adults between the ages of 18 and 65, with a BMI of at least 27 kg/m², were assigned to one of two treatment groups: IGB only or IGB + semaglutide. Subcutaneous injections of semaglutide were administered with increasing dosages on a weekly basis in the second month and were continued after the removal of the intragastric balloon. All participants were monitored, and results were recorded at 3, 6, and 12 months. Forty patients completed the study (n = 20 per group). The IGB + semaglutide group lost more weight than the IGB only group at 3, 6, and 12 months, with statistically significant differences at 6 months (29.09 ± 3.45 kg vs. 18.35 ± 2.80 kg, p < 0.001) and 12 months (33.03 ± 3.55 kg vs. 15.56 ± 2.50 kg, p < 0.001). After intragastric balloon removal at 6 months, the IGB only group regained previously lost weight while the IGB + semaglutide group continued to lose weight (2.79 ± 1.74 vs. -3.94 ± 2.16, p < 0.001). Adjunctive semaglutide therapy with intragastric balloon (IGB) optimizes weight loss, while enhancing the sustainability achieved with intragastric ballooning alone. Introduction: Obesity represents a global public health burden. It is typically interrelated to a plethora of complications that predispose to avoidable morbidity and mortality [1]. The rates of obesity worldwide have more than doubled over the past 35 years, with adolescent obesity having quadrupled [2]. While lifestyle intervention remains a cornerstone in the management of obesity, its effectiveness is often modest, with long-term studies such as Look AHEAD showing that approximately 50% of participants achieved ≥ 5% weight loss and almost one-third of participants achieved ≥ 10% weight loss at 8 years. These outcomes depend heavily on sustained patient engagement and adherence to behavioral changes [3]. Obesity remains an underdiagnosed and undertreated condition [4]. Classically, treatment is initiated from the least invasive and may be escalated towards pharmacotherapy, endoscopic bariatric interventions, and lastly, surgical intervention. At present, the gold standard management for the unsuccessful medical treatment of obesity is surgical intervention, providing unrivalled weight loss. These interventions include but are not limited to the adjustable gastric band, sleeve gastrectomy, and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass [5]. Despite providing considerable weight loss, only between 0.5 and 1% of eligible patients undergo bariatric surgery [6]. Perhaps this may be in part due to high cost, concerns related to surgical intervention, and lack of access to bariatric centers [7]. Endoscopic bariatric therapy offers a less invasive option for patients reluctant to undergo surgery and includes various procedures such as space-occupying devices, restrictive procedures, and aspiration therapies [8]. Space-occupying devices refer to Intragastric balloons (IGB) that are usually temporary, endoscopically placed air or fluid-filled balloons, resulting in fullness that leads to weight loss [8]. Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), has emerged as an effective medical treatment alternative for obesity. Its subcutaneous administration has demonstrated significant success in promoting weight loss in adults with type 2 diabetes [9]. It is approved as a supplemental therapy for overweight and obese adults, in conjunction with a calorie-restricted diet and enhanced physical activity in adults with a baseline BMI ≥ 30 or ≥ 27 kg/m² with at least one weight-related comorbidity, across the USA, Canada, Europe, and the UK [10]. This study explores the use of intragastric balloons (IGBs), highlighting their applications, efficacy, and role in the management of obesity. While IGBs are an established endoscopic intervention for weight loss, the impact of combining IGB insertion with semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, remains unclear. Therefore, we aim to evaluate the efficacy of this combined approach on weight reduction.

Study Design and Setting: This prospective comparative study was conducted at Alexandria Main University Hospital, Alexandria, and included adult patients diagnosed with overweight or obesity who were scheduled for endoscopic intragastric balloon (IGB) placement.

Patient Selection: Eligible participants were men and women aged 18 to 65 years with a body mass index (BMI) of 27 kg/m² or higher. All patients provided informed consent prior to enrollment. Exclusion criteria comprised a history of previous bariatric surgery, contraindications to IGB insertion or semaglutide use, the presence of gastrointestinal disorders such as inflammatory bowel disease or gastroparesis, severe organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, or cardiac), pregnancy, and current use of other anti-obesity medications.

Randomization and Group Allocation: Following screening and informed consent, patients were randomized into two equal groups, with 25 participants allocated to each group. Study recruitment was closed once complete 12-month follow-up data were obtained for 20 patients in each group. The random allocation sequence was generated through an online tool (http://www.randomizer.org), which generated a randomized list of patient identification codes. Allocation was concealed using sealed, opaque envelopes, prepared and managed by an independent third party to prevent selection bias. IGB only, the control group, underwent intragastric balloon (IGB) insertion alone, while the intervention group received IGB insertion in combination with subcutaneous semaglutide injections. This was an open-label trial; hence, neither participants nor investigators were blinded to group assignments. The nature of the interventions precluded effective blinding.

Intervention Protocol: All IGB procedures were performed under conscious sedation by an experienced endoscopist, using endoscopically placed, liquid-filled intragastric balloons (Spatz3 ®) with a fill volume ranging from 400 to 700 ml of saline and methylene blue, adjusted according to the fundus size as assessed by endoscopy. The IGB was maintained intragastric for six months, after which it was removed endoscopically. Patients in the IGB + semaglutide group received the Semaglutide (Ozempic ®) injections following a structured titration and administration schedule. The regimen began with an initial dose of 0.5 mg once weekly during the second month. The dose was then escalated to the full therapeutic dose of 1 mg once weekly during the third and fourth months. This dose was maintained during this period, then paused for the fifth and sixth months while the intragastric balloon was still in place and subsequently removed after the sixth month. Semaglutide was reintroduced at 1 mg once weekly during the seventh and eighth months, after which the therapy was discontinued. All participants in both groups were instructed to adhere to a standardized dietary protocol, beginning with a liquid diet in the first week post-IGB insertion, progressing to a soft diet, and subsequently transitioning to a structured hypocaloric solid diet. Dietary counseling and lifestyle modification support, including recommendations for regular physical activity, were provided by a dietitian throughout the study period.

Semaglutide Regimen: The Semaglutide dosing regimen in this study was tailored to optimize the synergistic effects with the intragastric balloon while maintaining patient safety and tolerability. Starting with an initial dose of 0.5 mg weekly allowed gradual dose escalation to the therapeutic dose of 1 mg weekly, minimizing the risk of adverse effects commonly associated with higher doses. The decision to avoid reaching the maximum dose of 2 mg was based on the hypothesis that 1 mg would provide sufficient efficacy when combined with the gastric balloon. The dosing schedule was strategically designed to be given in the critical period of balloon placement, specifically during the second to fourth months and after balloon removal in the seventh and eighth months. While the maximum effect of the balloon is observed in the first month, our intention was to support and sustain the balloon’s weight loss effect after this initial peak period (2nd to 4th months). Continued Semaglutide adaptations and on for 2 months post-balloon removal aimed to sustain weight loss, support metabolic adaptations, and facilitate behavioral changes necessary for long-term maintenance (7th & 8th months). The dosing schedule includes a 2-month hiatus during the fifth and sixth months, corresponding with the continuation of gastric balloon therapy during a total 6-month period. This pause was intentional and designed to support and sustain balloon efficacy after the initial phase, allowing the Semaglutide to be reintroduced after balloon removal in the seventh and eighth months to consolidate weight loss and support behavioral change. This regimen balances efficacy, safety, and patient adherence by providing targeted pharmacological support aligned with the clinical course of gastric balloon therapy.

Outcome Measures and Follow-Up: Primary outcome: The percentage change in body weight from baseline to 12 months after intervention is the primary outcome investigated in this study. Weight and BMI were measured at baseline and then at 3, 6, and 12 months. Total Body Weight Loss (TBWL) and Excess Weight Loss (EWL) are the two principal metrics used to assess the effectiveness of weight loss, especially in a bariatric setting. TBWL is the absolute reduction in body weight, calculated as a percentage of the preoperative weight by dividing the difference between the initial and current weights by the initial weight, and then multiplying by 100. In contrast, EWL is the proportion of weight loss relative to the excess weight above an “ideal weight,” using the formula: (preoperative weight minus current weight) divided by (preoperative weight minus ideal weight), also multiplied by 100. The “ideal weight” refers to the body weight corresponding to a body mass index (BMI) of 25 kg/m², calculated as 25 times the square of the person’s height in meters. Secondary Outcome: The secondary outcomes investigated in the present study included safety, specifically the incidence and nature of treatment-related complications associated with the intragastric balloon and Semaglutide combination therapy. This also includes monitoring adverse events such as nausea, vomiting, gastroparesis, pancreatitis, and any other clinically relevant complications throughout the study duration. Follow up: Adherence to the treatment protocol, patient-reported tolerance, serious complications, and any adverse events were prospectively recorded at each scheduled visit, although a specific validated nausea scoring tool was not employed. Clinical assessments and patient self-reports guided the monitoring process. We define serious complications as any adverse events requiring discontinuation of the current plan, hospitalization, or posing significant health risks occurring within the study follow-up period of 12 months. The primary endpoint was defined as the difference in mean weight loss between the two groups at the end of the twelve-month follow-up period.

Sample Size Calculation: The sample size was calculated based on detecting a clinically meaningful difference in mean weight loss between the IGB-only group and the IGB + Semaglutide at the 6-month follow-up. Assuming a mean difference of approximately 10.74 kg (29.09 kg vs. 18.35 kg), with a standard deviation of approximately 3.5 kg based on preliminary data and prior literature, a two-sided alpha level of 0.05 and 80% power, the minimum required sample size per group was estimated to be 17 participants. To account for potential dropouts and losses to follow-up, 25 participants were initially recruited per group, ensuring that at least 20 completed the study in each arm, thus maintaining sufficient power for the final analysis. This sample size is justified to detect the significant differences observed in weight loss outcomes and supports the validity of the study findings.

Statistical Analysis of the Data: Data were analyzed using the IBM SPSS software package version 20.0. (Armonk, NY: IBM Corp, released in 2011). Categorical data were represented as numbers and percentages. The chi-square test was applied to compare the two groups. Alternatively, Fisher’s Exact correction test was applied when more than 20% of the cells had an expected count less than 5. For continuous data, they were tested for normality by the Shapiro-Wilk test. Quantitative data were expressed as range (minimum and maximum), mean, standard deviation, and median. Student t-test was used to compare two groups for normally distributed quantitative variables, while ANOVA with repeated measures was used for normally distributed quantitative variables, to compare between more than two periods or stages, and Post Hoc test (Bonferroni adjusted) for pairwise comparisons. On the other hand, the Mann-Whitney test was used to compare two groups for not normally distributed quantitative variables. The significance of the results obtained was judged at the 5% level. An intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis was performed, including all randomized participants regardless of dropout status.

Results: A total of 40 patients were ultimately enrolled in the study and evenly assigned to two groups: IGB only and IGB + semaglutide, with 20 patients in each group. Initially, approximately 25 patients were recruited per group to account for potential withdrawals or loss to follow-up. During the study, 3 patients from the IGB-only group and 2 patients from the IGB + semaglutide group discontinued follow-up after balloon removal. One patient cited living more than three hours from the center as the reason, while the other four voluntarily withdrew because they were satisfied with their weight loss outcomes and felt no further medical supervision was necessary. Importantly, these voluntary discontinuations were based on perceived satisfactory results rather than inadequate weight loss, minimizing potential bias. Complications: During the study, no serious complications occurred in either group that required discontinuation of semaglutide or removal of the gastric balloon. All patients also received standard post-IGB insertion medications, such as proton pump inhibitors and analgesics, to enhance tolerance and reduce early side effects. Discussion: Given the significant increase in prevalence and burden of obesity globally, there is a need to explore and establish available treatment modalities and their outcomes. As of 2021, approximately 1 in 8 people worldwide were living with obesity [11]. With 42% of United States adults classified as obese and obesity-related healthcare expenses estimated at $173 billion annually, effective and sustainable interventions are necessary [5]. Currently, most studies assess the effectiveness of individual therapies, leaving limited evidence on the results of combination therapy. This study was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of combining endoscopic and pharmaceutical interventions, including intragastric balloon and semaglutide injections. Our results demonstrate the following findings: Both the IGB only group and the IGB + semaglutide group significantly lost weight compared to baseline; the IGB + semaglutide group had a significantly higher total body weight loss (TBWL) and excess weight loss (EWL) percentage when compared to the IGB only group, primarily at 6 and 12 months; the IGB only group had significant weight regain in comparison to the IGB + semaglutide group after intragastric balloon removal. The IGB only group and the IGB + semaglutide group demonstrated statistically significant reductions compared to baseline body weight of 9.41% and 11.44% at 3 months, 15.88% and 24.85% at 6 months, and 13.47% and 28.21% at 12 months, respectively. In comparison, a multicenter clinical trial on IGB use reported a total body weight loss of 8.5% at 3 months, 11.8% at 6 months, and 13.3% at 12 months, while semaglutide studies have shown approximately 10.9% weight loss at 6 months and 13.9% at 12 months [12, 13]. Both the IGB only group and the IGB + semaglutide group achieved the most substantial weight reduction during the first six months, aligning with the established therapeutic window for IGB therapy [14]. The IGB only group achieved its lowest weight at 6 months. The IGB + semaglutide group achieved maximal weight loss at 12 months following balloon removal. This pattern is likely due to the complementary mechanisms of both therapies. The IGB leads to weight reduction by mechanically obstructing gastric volume and stimulating satiety via mechanoreceptors [15]. Following balloon removal, semaglutide sustains satiety and appetite suppression via GLP-1 receptor activation [16]. The IGB + semaglutide group continued weight loss demonstrates the efficacy of semaglutide therapy, and its ability to not only sustain but also further weight loss subsequent to balloon removal. Semaglutide injections were given at 2, 3, and 4 months, with injections at the 5th and 6th month withheld, followed by a booster dose at the 7th and 8th month. This sustained weight loss suggests semaglutide therapy may overcome the 6-month plateau following 10–13% weight reduction often observed in IGB ballooning due to metabolic adaptation and hormonal changes [5, 17]. This synergistic effect persisted following balloon removal and despite semaglutide dosage reduction, emphasizing the efficacy and cost efficiency of this combined therapy. These results demonstrate the advantages of combined IGB and semaglutide therapy on early weight loss and sustained appetite suppression compared to IGB alone. When comparing both treatment groups, the IGB + semaglutide group had a significantly higher TBWL and EWL than the IGB only group, specifically at 6 and 12 months. Even though both groups did lose significant weight at 3 months compared to baseline, the IGB + semaglutide group showed an increased weight loss that was not statistically significant in comparison to the IGB only group. Semaglutide induces weight loss through its interactions with GLP-1 receptors that directly and indirectly regulate the hypothalamus and hindbrain, which are brain areas involved in appetite mediation [18]. Semaglutide’s effects on weight reduction are commonly observed within the first four weeks of treatment, yet its maximal effect is achieved by week 60 [17, 19]. This may explain why weight reduction at 3 months was evident in both the IGB-only group and the IGB + semaglutide group, yet this difference was not found to be significant until 6 and 12 months of therapy. Placement of the intragastric balloon triggers weight loss through a restrictive mechanism using space-occupancy [20]. This modifies gastric accommodation and emptying, which further prompts feelings of satiety through gastrointestinal neurohormonal pathways [20]. Given semaglutide’s ability to delay gastric emptying and suppress appetite [5], along with the intragastric balloon’s space-occupying mechanism, this treatment approach may exhibit a synergistic effect on weight loss. title: Cardiometabolic Parameter Change by Weight Regain on Tirzepatide Withdrawal in Adults With Obesity: A Post Hoc Analysis of the SURMOUNT-4 Trial.
abstract: IMPORTANCE: In the SURMOUNT-4 trial, most adults with obesity who had tirzepatide withdrawn following a 36-week treatment regained weight. The association between the degree of weight regain and cardiometabolic parameters after tirzepatide withdrawal is unknown. | OBJECTIVE: To assess changes in cardiometabolic parameters by degree of weight regain after withdrawal of tirzepatide. | DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This post hoc analysis of the SURMOUNT-4 trial included tirzepatide-treated participants with 10% or greater weight reduction at week 36 initially randomized to placebo. Data were collected from March 2021 to May 2023, and data were analyzed from February 2024 to March 2025. | INTERVENTIONS: After 36 weeks of tirzepatide treatment (maximum tolerated dose of 10 mg or 15 mg), participants were randomized 1:1 to continue tirzepatide or to switch to placebo for 52 weeks (week 36 to 88). | MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Changes from week 36 to week 88 in cardiometabolic parameters on tirzepatide withdrawal were assessed by the degree of weight regain at week 88 as a percentage of weight lost while receiving tirzepatide from week 0 to 36: less than 25%, 25% to less than 50%, 50% to less than 75%, and 75% or more. | RESULTS: Of 308 included participants, 219 (71.1%) were female, 89 (28.9%) were male, and the mean (SD) age was 47.1 (12.2) years. There were 54 participants in the less than 25% weight regain group, 77 in the 25% to less than 50% group, 103 in the 50% to less than 75% group, and 74 in the 75% or more group. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were similar across categories. During the initial 36 weeks of tirzepatide treatment, participants' weight decreased and cardiometabolic parameters improved. After withdrawal of tirzepatide, from week 36 to week 88, the mean change in waist circumference increased by weight regain category (<25% weight regain, 0.8 cm; 95% CI, -1.0 to 2.6; 25% to <50%, 5.4 cm; 95% CI, 4.0-6.8; 50% to <75%, 10.1 cm; 95% CI, 8.9-11.3; ≥75%, 14.7 cm; 95% CI, 12.7-16.7; P < .001), as did systolic blood pressure (6.8 mm Hg [95% CI, 3.9-9.7], 7.3 mm Hg [95% CI, 4.8-9.8], 9.6 mm Hg [95% CI, 7.1-12.1], and 10.4 mm Hg [95% CI, 8.0-12.8], respectively; P = .002), non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (-0.4% [95% CI, -7.3 to 6.5], 1.6% [95% CI, -2.3 to 5.5], 8.4% [95% CI, 3.9-12.9], and 10.8% [95% CI, 5.3-16.3], respectively), hemoglobin A1c (0.14% [95% CI, 0.06-0.22], 0.15% [95% CI, 0.09-0.21], 0.27% [95% CI, 0.21-0.33], and 0.35% [95% CI, 0.29-0.41], respectively; P < .001), and fasting insulin (-4.0% [95% CI, -20.7 to 12.7], 15.4% [95% CI, 2.3-28.5], 46.2% [95% CI, 29.5-62.9], and 26.3% [95% CI, 9.6-43.0], respectively). These findings underscore the importance of continued obesity treatment. | TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04660643.

TITLE: Cardiometabolic Parameter Change by Weight Regain on Tirzepatide Withdrawal in Adults With Obesity

ABSTRACT: Does the degree of weight regain following tirzepatide withdrawal affect long-term cardiometabolic benefits in individuals with obesity or overweight? In this post hoc analysis of the SURMOUNT-4 randomized clinical trial including 308 participants, participants experienced weight reduction and improvement in cardiometabolic parameters after a 36-week tirzepatide treatment. One year after tirzepatide withdrawal, a higher degree of weight regain was associated with a greater reversal of initial improvements in waist circumference, blood pressure, non–high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, glycemic parameters, and insulin resistance. In this post hoc analysis, on tirzepatide withdrawal, greater reversal of initial cardiometabolic benefits was observed in participants who regained 25% or more of their initial weight reduction vs those who did not.
